subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change
title: Vikram's Discovery: Why Petrol Costs More Some Days
hook: Every week, Vikram's mum complains about petrol prices. Why does ₹100 sometimes buy 5 litres and sometimes only 4.8 litres? Vikram discovers the global oil market.

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: Class 11 student from Mumbai curious about global commodities

characters.name: Mr. Desai
characters.role: Economics teacher who explains commodity trading

slides.title: The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change
slides.storyContext: At a petrol pump in Mumbai, Vikram notices the price board: ₹106.31 per litre (Petrol). Last month, it was ₹102.50. He asks his aunt Asha, a petroleum engineer: 'Why does the price jump around so much? Is the oil company greedy?'

image.alt: The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: The Global Oil Supply Chain
slides.storyContext: 'It's not greed,' Asha explains over chai. 'India produces only 10% of the oil it needs. We import 90% from the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Iraq, UAE), Russia, and Africa. The price of that oil is set in a global market—in USD—on exchanges in New York and London. When global prices rise, petrol becomes expensive in India too.' Vikram: 'But petrol was ₹102 last month and ₹106 this month. What changed in one month?' Mr. Desai (Asha's friend) joins the conversation: 'Supply and demand, geopolitics, and currency. Let me show you.'

image.alt: The Global Oil Supply Chain — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Asha's Lesson: India's Oil Dependence
slides.storyContext: Asha pulls out a world map on her tablet. 'Look, Vikram. India's oil production is only here—Gujarat, Bombay High offshore field. We produce about 25 million tonnes per year, but we CONSUME 240 million tonnes. So we import 215 million tonnes from outside. It's like you earn ₹25,000 a month but spend ₹240,000—you need to borrow ₹215,000. Now imagine that borrowed money's price changes daily. That's India's situation with oil.'

image.alt: Asha's Lesson: India's Oil Dependence — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: What Determines Oil Price: Global Supply & Demand

points.label: Global Oil Supply
points.text: Oil is produced by ~150 countries. The largest producers: USA (~13 million barrels/day), Saudi Arabia (~10 m b/d), Russia (~10 m b/d), Canada, China, Iraq. OPEC (13 countries, including Saudi Arabia) controls ~30% of global supply and acts as a cartel—they can cut production to raise prices or increase it to lower prices.

points.label: Global Demand
points.text: Cars, trucks, ships, factories, power plants all need oil. USA (~20 m b/d), China (~15 m b/d), India (~5 m b/d), Japan, Germany are the largest consumers. As economies grow, demand rises. During recessions, demand falls.

points.label: The Price Mechanism
points.text: If OPEC cuts production (less supply) and global demand stays high, oil price rises. If demand drops (recession) but supply stays high, oil price falls. Price swings until supply = demand.

points.label: Crude Oil Price Benchmarks
points.text: Brent Crude (UK North Sea, ~Opec benchmark) and WTI (USA, ~lighter oil). On any day, they trade on commodity exchanges. Brent might be $85/barrel; WTI might be $80/barrel. India primarily imports Brent-type crude.

example.problem: In January 2023, Brent crude was $85/barrel. In December 2023, it was $75/barrel. If Brent dropped $10, and 1 barrel = ~159 litres, roughly how much cheaper should Indian petrol be?
example.solution: Cost drop = $10 ÷ 159 ≈ $0.063 per litre, or ₹5–6 per litre (at 1 USD ≈ ₹83). This is the CRUDE cost drop. But Indian petrol price includes excise tax (~₹25/litre), state tax (~₹12–25/litre), distribution, and retailer margin. So retail petrol might drop only ₹3–4 per litre when crude drops $10. The rest of the price is TAX and MARGIN, not crude cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oil is like any commodity traded globally. When global demand is high and supply is low, price rises. When demand is weak (recession) or supply is high (OPEC increases production), price falls. India, importing 90% of its oil, feels every global price swing.

slides.title: Example: Supply Shock in 2020
slides.storyContext: Vikram asks: 'What happened during COVID in 2020?' Mr. Desai explains: 'That was the biggest demand shock in decades. People stopped driving, flying, factories shut down. Demand dropped 30 million barrels/day instantly. But supply couldn't fall that fast—oil wells keep producing.'

example.problem: In April 2020, global oil demand fell from 100 million b/d to 70 million b/d. Supply was still 95 million b/d. What happened to price?
example.solution: Supply (95) > Demand (70), so there was excess of 25 million b/d. Buyers said 'we don't need this much' and offered lower prices. Price collapsed to $20/barrel (from $50). Producers had to pay to store excess oil because tankers were full and storage ran out.

slides.inSimpleWords: When demand drops suddenly (recession, pandemic), supply can't react instantly. Prices crash because buyers don't want excess supply.

image.alt: Example: Supply Shock in 2020 — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: OPEC's Power: Cartel Behavior and Price Control

points.label: What Is OPEC?
points.text: Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. Members: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Iraq, Iran, Venezuela, Algeria, Angola, Libya, Ecuador, Gabon, Nigeria, Guinea Equatorial. Together, they pump ~30 million barrels/day (about 30% of global supply).

points.label: Cartel Behavior
points.text: OPEC members agree on production quotas. If they cut production together, oil becomes scarce, and prices rise. If they increase production, prices fall. Saudi Arabia is the 'swing producer'—it cuts or raises production to keep prices in its target range (e.g., $80–100/barrel).

points.label: Historical Examples
points.text: 1973 Arab-Israel War: OPEC cut supply, oil spiked to $12/barrel (massive shock). 2008 Financial Crisis: demand crashed, oil fell to $30/barrel. 2020 COVID: demand collapsed, oil went NEGATIVE (producers paid to take oil off their hands). 2022 Ukraine war: Russia's supply threatened, oil spiked to $120/barrel.

points.label: Limits to OPEC's Power
points.text: Non-OPEC production (USA shale oil, UK North Sea) can't be controlled by OPEC. If OPEC raises prices too high, non-OPEC producers ramp up, flooding the market. If OPEC cuts, but demand is weak, prices still fall.

example.problem: In 2022, Russia (non-OPEC, but huge exporter at ~10 m b/d) invaded Ukraine. Buyers feared Russian supply would be cut (sanctions). OPEC did NOT cut production to compensate. What happened to oil prices?
example.solution: Oil spiked from ~$95/barrel (pre-invasion) to $120/barrel. Why? Loss of Russian supply + uncertainty created panic buying. OPEC could have raised production to ease the panic, but they didn't—they let prices spike. Why? Because higher prices benefit Saudi Arabia, UAE, and other OPEC members financially. So petrol in India jumped to ₹120+ per litre overnight, and Indians paid more for petrol, while oil companies (and OPEC) profited.

slides.inSimpleWords: OPEC is like a mafia for oil. 13 countries agree to cut production if prices fall too low. This raises prices and helps their economies. But it also hurts oil importers like India. When OPEC cuts supply, Indians pay more at the petrol pump.

slides.title: The Saudi Arabia Gamble: Production Cuts
slides.storyContext: Asha tells Vikram: 'In 2023, OPEC made a big move. Saudi Arabia announced a 1 million barrel/day cut. I watched the markets that day—oil prices jumped from $82 to $86 instantly. One announcement by Saudi, and oil became more expensive for the entire world. That's power.'

image.alt: The Saudi Arabia Gamble: Production Cuts — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: How OPEC Decisions Ripple: A Real-Time Example
slides.storyContext: Mr. Desai shows Vikram a timeline. 'OPEC meets in Vienna, announces a cut, and within hours traders buy oil contracts expecting scarcity. Prices jump. Within days, Indians see ₹2–3 jump at the pump. No one in India voted for this, but global cartels decide our petrol price. That's the power of being dependent on imports.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A decision in Vienna (OPEC HQ) ripples to Mumbai petrol pumps within hours. India has no control but feels the full impact.

slides.title: Geopolitical Shocks and Oil Prices

points.label: Wars and Sanctions
points.text: If a war threatens oil supply (e.g., Russia-Ukraine, Iran tensions, Middle East conflicts), oil prices spike immediately due to fear. Even if actual supply doesn't change, the EXPECTATION of disruption raises prices. Historical: Gulf War (1990–91), Iraq invasion (2003), Iran sanctions (2018).

points.label: Currency Fluctuations
points.text: Oil is priced in USD. If INR weakens vs. USD (1 USD = ₹90 instead of ₹83), Indian petrol becomes MORE expensive. If INR strengthens, petrol becomes cheaper. This is separate from global crude prices.

points.label: Economic Cycles
points.text: Recessions reduce oil demand → prices fall (e.g., 2008, 2020). Strong growth increases demand → prices rise (e.g., 2004–2007, 2021–2022). India's growth, China's growth directly affect global demand.

points.label: Climate & Natural Disasters
points.text: Hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico can disrupt US offshore oil production. Droughts affect refinery cooling. These supply shocks can spike prices temporarily.

example.problem: In 2022, the INR fell from ₹75/USD to ₹83/USD. Global crude was stable at $100/barrel. If ₹1 litre of petrol was ₹100 when INR was ₹75/USD, how much should it cost when INR is ₹83/USD?
example.solution: Original: $100/barrel ÷ 159 litres/barrel ≈ $0.628/litre × ₹75 ≈ ₹47. After depreciation: $0.628/litre × ₹83 ≈ ₹52.1. So even with STABLE global crude, petrol in India becomes ₹5 more expensive just because the rupee weakened. This is on top of crude price changes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Geopolitics (wars, sanctions, trade tensions) affect oil prices instantly because traders fear supply cuts. Currency fluctuations also affect Indian petrol prices—if rupee weakens, imports (including oil) become expensive.

slides.title: The Ukraine War: Geopolitics in Action
slides.storyContext: Mr. Desai shows Vikram a chart: 'February 24, 2022—Russia invades Ukraine. That same day, oil jumped $15/barrel. The markets didn't know how much Russian oil would be cut, so traders panicked and bid prices up. Asha's company had to renegotiate supply contracts instantly. Petrol in India jumped ₹15 per litre in two weeks.'

image.alt: The Ukraine War: Geopolitics in Action — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Example: Rupee Depreciation Impact
slides.storyContext: Vikram checks the rupee-dollar rate on his phone. 'Aunt, the rupee was ₹80/USD last month and ₹85/USD today. Does that mean petrol got more expensive just because of that?'

example.problem: On Day 1: Crude ₹47/litre (at ₹80/USD). On Day 2: Crude $0.628/litre × ₹85/USD = ₹53.4/litre. If all other costs (tax, refining) stayed the same, by how much did petrol price rise just due to rupee depreciation?
example.solution: Crude portion rose by ₹6.4/litre just from rupee falling. If petrol was ₹100/litre on Day 1 with ₹47 crude, it would be ₹106.4/litre on Day 2 (assuming taxes and refining didn't change). So currency matters even when global crude prices don't move.

slides.inSimpleWords: A weak rupee makes imported oil more expensive directly. This adds to price swings from global supply-demand.

image.alt: Example: Rupee Depreciation Impact — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Currency Wars and Oil: An Indian Perspective
slides.storyContext: Vikram realizes: 'So India's rupee weakness makes everything imported expensive—not just petrol, but electronics, clothes, everything from abroad?' Asha nods. 'Exactly. And oil is the biggest import by volume. A 10% rupee fall can push petrol prices up ₹10 per litre alone, without global crude prices moving. It's like a hidden tax on all of us importers.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rupee weakness hits Indians hardest in oil prices because oil is imported and consumed by everyone—cars, trucks, buses, generators.

slides.title: How Petrol Prices Reach Indian Pumps

points.label: Step 1: Global Crude Purchase
points.text: Indian government's Petroleum Ministry or state-run refineries (IOC, HPCL, BPCL) buy crude oil from global markets (Saudi Arabia, etc.) at Brent/WTI prices.

points.label: Step 2: Refining
points.text: Crude is shipped to India's refineries (Jamnagar, Kochi, Baroda, etc.). Refineries process crude into petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG, etc. Refining adds ₹5–10/litre to the cost.

points.label: Step 3: Taxes
points.text: Central Excise Tax (~₹25–32/litre, set by FM in budget) + State VAT/Excise (~₹12–25/litre, varies by state). These taxes are HUGE—they make up ~50% of petrol price.

points.label: Step 4: Distribution & Retail Margin
points.text: Transport to petrol pumps, storage, and pump operator's margin (~₹3–5/litre). Finally, the pump price is calculated: Crude Cost + Refining + Taxes + Distribution + Retailer Margin.

points.label: Daily Price Changes
points.text: The government allows petrol prices to change daily based on global crude prices. So ₹106.31 today, ₹106.45 tomorrow, ₹106.12 the day after—tiny swings reflect global crude swings.

example.problem: Breakdown of a ₹100 petrol litre in Mumbai (approximate, 2023): Crude ₹45, Refining ₹8, Excise ₹27, State VAT ₹15, Distribution ₹3, Retail Margin ₹2. If global crude rises to push 'Crude' to ₹48, what's the new petrol price?
example.solution: ₹48 + ₹8 + ₹27 + ₹15 + ₹3 + ₹2 = ₹103. A ₹3/litre increase because of ₹3 rise in global crude. But notice: crude is only 45–48% of the price. Taxes are 42% (₹42/₹100). So even if crude dropped 20%, petrol price would drop only ~₹9–10 (20% of 45), not 20% of ₹100.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you pay ₹100 for petrol, roughly ₹45 goes to oil producers (global crude cost), ₹42 goes to taxes (government), and ₹13 covers refining and distribution. When global crude rises by $10/barrel, your petrol price rises by ₹5–6, not ₹20. Taxes and refining make up the rest.

slides.title: Inside an Indian Refinery
slides.storyContext: Asha takes Vikram to a refinery in Gujarat. 'Look, this is where crude oil becomes petrol. We buy crude at global prices, refine it (add cost), then ship to pumps across India. Every step adds cost—shipping, storage, taxes at the state border. By the time it reaches Mumbai, it's more expensive than when it left Saudi Arabia.'

image.alt: Inside an Indian Refinery — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Example: Tax Breakdown Matters
slides.storyContext: Vikram sees the price at the Mumbai pump: ₹106.31. He asks: 'Of this, how much is tax?'

example.problem: If crude is $85/barrel (≈₹46/litre), refining is ₹8/litre, and total petrol price is ₹106, what are the taxes?
example.solution: Taxes = ₹106 − ₹46 − ₹8 − (distribution + margin ₹5) = ₹47/litre. So ₹47 out of ₹106 (44%) is pure TAX. This is why petrol doesn't drop much when crude falls—taxes don't fall with crude.

slides.inSimpleWords: Government taxes on petrol make up a huge chunk of the price. When crude falls, taxes stay the same, so petrol price doesn't fall proportionally.

image.alt: Example: Tax Breakdown Matters — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Why Taxes Matter More Than Most Think
slides.storyContext: Mr. Desai tells Vikram: 'In budget speeches, ministers claim they're 'protecting consumers from global oil shocks.' But the truth? They silently raise excise tax during budget sessions, hiding increases inside 'rising crude.' If crude rises ₹3 and tax rises ₹2 silently, Indians blame global markets when it's actually their government taking more.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Government taxes on petrol are the biggest secret in oil pricing—they don't fall when crude falls, and they rise during budgets without headlines.

slides.title: A Real Oil Price Timeline: 2020–2024
slides.storyContext: Vikram looks up historical oil prices with Mr. Desai.

example.problem:
Timeline:
- Jan 2020: Brent $65/barrel, Petrol ₹71/litre (India)
- Apr 2020 (COVID): Brent $20/barrel, Petrol ₹59/litre
- Dec 2021: Brent $80/barrel, Petrol ₹95/litre
- June 2022 (Ukraine war): Brent $120/barrel, Petrol ₹120/litre
- Dec 2023: Brent $75/barrel, Petrol ₹100/litre

Why didn't petrol reach ₹59 in Dec 2023 when Brent was $75 (higher than $65 in Jan 2020)?
example.solution: Because taxes and refining costs ROSE over 4 years. In Jan 2020, Excise tax was ~₹21/litre. By Dec 2023, Excise tax was ~₹27–32/litre (increased by FM in budgets). Also, refining costs increased due to stranded assets (older refineries). So even though global crude was slightly cheaper, Indian petrol price remained ₹100 due to HIGHER TAXES. This is a political/policy choice—governments raise excise tax during budget to meet revenue targets, hiding it behind 'rising crude prices.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Global crude prices swung wildly: $20 in COVID, $120 in war, $75 now. But Indian petrol price changes were not proportional because taxes increased. So petrol stayed expensive even when global crude fell—governments silently raised taxes.

image.alt: A Real Oil Price Timeline: 2020–2024 — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Why Did Petrol Stay Expensive After COVID?
slides.storyContext: Vikram is confused. 'In April 2020, crude was $20 and petrol was ₹59. In Dec 2023, crude was $75 and petrol was ₹100. Shouldn't it have gone back to ₹71?' Mr. Desai smiles: 'Because your government raised taxes in the budgets of 2021, 2022, 2023. They collected extra tax revenue while crude was falling. A hidden increase.'

image.alt: Why Did Petrol Stay Expensive After COVID? — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: Challenge: Predict Petrol Prices
slides.storyContext:
Today, Brent crude is $85/barrel. Vikram reads the news:
- OPEC might cut production by 1 million barrels/day next month (bullish for prices)
- India's economy is slowing (bearish for demand)
- India's rupee is depreciating vs. USD (bullish for import costs)
- No major geopolitical shocks expected

Will petrol prices in India go UP or DOWN next month?

example.problem:
Factors:
Bullish: OPEC cuts (supply constraint), rupee depreciation
Bearish: India's economic slowdown (demand weakness)
Neutral: No geopolitical shock

What will dominate?
example.solution: Likely outcome: UPWARD pressure. OPEC cuts typically outweigh modest demand weakness. Also, rupee depreciation adds to petrol cost directly. Best-case scenario for Indians: OPEC's cut is smaller than expected (market overestimated), or global demand spikes (China reopens), eroding OPEC's pricing power. Worst-case: OPEC fully delivers the cut, rupee falls more, and petrol reaches ₹110+. But predicting commodity prices is hard—many factors interact.

slides.title: Challenge: Build a Price Model
slides.storyContext: Vikram wants to estimate petrol price himself: 'Aunt, give me crude price, I'll predict petrol.'

example.problem: If crude is $X/barrel, estimate the petrol price in India. Build a model using: Crude cost ≈ (X ÷ 159) × 83 (₹/litre, using ₹83/USD), Add refining ₹8, Add taxes ₹40 (excise + VAT), Add distribution ₹3. Total = Petrol price ₹.
example.solution: Formula: Petrol price ≈ (X ÷ 159) × 83 + 8 + 40 + 3 = (0.52 × X) + 51. So if crude is $85, petrol ≈ (0.52 × 85) + 51 = 44.2 + 51 = ₹95.2. Actual: ₹100–106. The difference is: state VAT varies (₹0–25/litre), state-to-state differences. But the formula gives a ballpark.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can build a rough model if you know crude price, refining cost, and tax rates. The formula helps you estimate, though actual prices vary by state.

slides.title: Challenge: Scenario Analysis
slides.storyContext: Vikram wants to see what happens if multiple factors change. 'What if OPEC cuts AND the rupee falls AND demand stays strong?'

example.problem: Scenario: Brent rises from $85 to $95 (OPEC cut). Rupee falls from ₹83 to ₹86/USD. Refining costs rise ₹2/litre due to supply tightness. Using the model, what's the new petrol price?
example.solution: Crude impact: (0.52 × 95) − (0.52 × 85) = 49.4 − 44.2 = +₹5.2. Rupee impact: (95/159) × (86 − 83) = 0.597 × 3 = +₹1.8. Refining: +₹2. Total: +₹9 on ₹95.2, so new petrol ≈ ₹104.2. Compare to current ₹100—a ₹4 jump.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiple factors compound. OPEC cuts, weak rupee, and rising refining costs can push petrol up ₹9–10 per litre quickly.

slides.title: Challenge: Spot the Hidden Tax Rise
slides.storyContext: Vikram's mum reads the budget: 'Excise tax on petrol raised by ₹2/litre.' Vikram asks: 'If crude stays at ₹46/litre, and this tax rises ₹2, shouldn't petrol price rise by exactly ₹2?'

example.problem: Current petrol: ₹100 (Crude ₹46 + Refining ₹8 + Excise ₹27 + VAT ₹15 + Distribution ₹4). Budget raises Excise by ₹2. New petrol price?
example.solution: Old: ₹46 + ₹8 + ₹27 + ₹15 + ₹4 = ₹100. New: ₹46 + ₹8 + ₹29 + ₹15 + ₹4 = ₹102. So petrol rises ₹2. But here's the trick: if crude simultaneously 'falls' ₹1 (news reports say 'crude dropped, but petrol stayed high'), people won't notice the tax was raised. They'll blame OPEC.

slides.inSimpleWords: Tax rises are easy to hide inside commodity price noise. A ₹2 tax rise offset by ₹1 crude fall looks like 'no change,' but it's actually a ₹2 tax hike.

slides.title: What We Learned: The Oil Market

points.text: Petrol prices are set in a global market (Brent, WTI). India imports 90% of its oil, so it's exposed to global supply-demand and geopolitics.
OPEC's 13 member countries control ~30% of global supply. By cutting production, they can raise prices globally—hurting oil importers like India.
Wars, sanctions, recessions, and currency fluctuations all affect oil prices instantly. A weak rupee makes petrol more expensive even if global crude is stable.
Indian petrol price = Crude Cost + Refining + Taxes + Distribution. Crude is ~45%, but taxes are ~42%. So crude price changes only move petrol price partially.
When Vikram's mum complains about petrol prices, she's really complaining about global forces (OPEC, geopolitics, rupee) and government taxes—not just 'oil company greed.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Your petrol price is shaped by global oil markets, OPEC decisions, currency swings, and government taxes. When petrol becomes expensive, it's often because of things beyond India's control—a war in the Middle East, OPEC's production cut, or rupee weakness. You can only watch and understand; you can't control it. But understanding it makes you a smarter financial citizen.

image.alt: What We Learned: The Oil Market — The Oil Market — Why Petrol Prices Change

slides.title: The Daily Price Dance
slides.storyContext: Vikram tracks petrol prices for a week. Monday: ₹105.50. Tuesday: ₹106.20. Wednesday: ₹105.75. 'It changes every day!' he exclaims. Asha smiles. 'Yes, because crude prices change every minute on global exchanges. India prices adjust daily to reflect this. One day's geopolitical shock becomes tomorrow's pump price.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Petrol prices shift daily because global crude markets react instantly to supply, demand, and geopolitical news.

slides.title: Renewable Energy & Oil's Future
slides.storyContext: Mr. Desai tells Vikram: 'Electric cars are coming. Solar is growing. In 50 years, oil may not dominate transport. But until then, India—lacking domestic oil—will remain dependent. So understanding oil markets is critical for your generation.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Oil will remain crucial for decades, so Indians must understand its markets, even as renewables grow.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Cricket Team Selection Mystery
hook: Arjun and Priya organize a school cricket tournament — but who counts as a team member?

slides.title: The Tournament Begins
slides.storyContext: Arjun is selecting his cricket team for the school tournament. He says, 'Our team has Raj, Karan, Priya, and Deepak.' Coach Ramesh asks: 'Arjun, what exactly do you mean by *your* team? Is it fixed? Can you list every member clearly?' Arjun realizes he needs a precise way to describe his group.

image.alt: The Tournament Begins — Sets

slides.title: The Ambiguous Team
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Arjun, is your team 'the best players' or 'the taller players'?' Arjun frowns. 'Well... Raj is good at batting, Karan is tall, Priya is fast... it's not clear.' Coach Ramesh interjects: 'That's the problem. 'Good' and 'tall' are subjective. Different people might disagree. To make a team fixed, you need a clear rule that everyone agrees on.'

image.alt: The Ambiguous Team — Sets

slides.title: What is a Set?
slides.storyContext: Coach Ramesh explains: 'A set is just a well-defined collection of distinct objects. In our cricket context, your team is a set.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects called elements.

points.label: Well-defined
points.text: For any object, we can clearly say whether it belongs or doesn't belong.

points.label: Distinct
points.text: No element repeats in a set — we list each only once.

points.label: Notation
points.text: We use capital letters: A, B, C. Elements go in braces: A = {1, 2, 3}.

example.problem: Is 'tall players' a valid set?
example.solution: No — 'tall' is vague. We can't agree on who is tall. A valid set might be {players with height > 180 cm} if we can measure.

slides.inSimpleWords: A set is a clearly defined group where each member either is or is not in it — no maybe.

slides.title: Making the Team Precise
slides.storyContext: Coach Ramesh says: 'Arjun, state your rule clearly. Do you mean: 'Players selected for the tournament squad' or 'Players with batting average > 30'?' Arjun thinks and says: 'The players selected for the tournament squad: Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak.' Priya nods. 'Good. Now everyone can verify if someone is in the team or not—they're on the official list or they're not.'

image.alt: Making the Team Precise — Sets

slides.title: Three-Team Scenario
slides.storyContext: Coach adds: 'Notice, Arjun, that Raj appears in multiple teams I create—he's in the batting team AND the fielding team. In a set world, that's fine. We can have overlaps. The key is: every team has a clear definition and a fixed list.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A player can belong to multiple sets (e.g., both batting AND bowling teams). Sets just need to be clearly defined.

slides.title: Representing Sets: Two Methods
slides.storyContext: Priya records the team two ways. Arjun says the names out loud (she writes them), and Coach writes rules on the board.

points.label: Roster Form
points.text: List all elements: A = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak}.

points.label: Set-builder Form
points.text: Write a rule: A = {x | x is a member of our team}.

points.label: Set-builder shorthand
points.text: A = {x | x ∈ cricket team of Class 11A}.

example.problem: Write the set of even single-digit natural numbers both ways.
example.solution: Roster: {2, 4, 6, 8}. Set-builder: {x | x is even and 1 < x < 10}.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can write a set by listing items or by giving a rule that picks them.

slides.title: Example: Roster vs. Set-builder
slides.storyContext: Arjun lists his team in roster form. Coach shows him set-builder form.

example.problem: Arjun's cricket team: Roster: {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera}. Write set-builder form.
example.solution: Set-builder: {x | x is in Arjun's cricket team} or more formally, {x | x ∈ S} where S is the official squad list. Or {x | x passed the skill trials and was selected}.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roster form lists names; set-builder form gives the rule that defines membership.

slides.title: Empty Set and Special Sets
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'What if no one shows up to a training session?' Coach says, 'That's the empty set — nothing in it.'

points.label: Empty set
points.text: The set with no elements: ∅ or { }.

points.label: Singleton set
points.text: A set with one element: {5}.

points.label: Finite set
points.text: A set with finitely many elements: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

points.label: Infinite set
points.text: A set with infinitely many elements: ℕ = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}.

example.problem: Is {x | x is a natural number and x < 1} empty?
example.solution: Yes — no natural number is less than 1, so this is ∅.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some sets are empty, some have one item, some have many, some go on forever.

slides.title: Special Sets in Sports
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Can a team have zero players?' Coach nods. 'Yes, it's the empty set. Also: a singleton set is one player (like when someone is injured and we have only one substitute). Finite sets have a fixed count. And there are infinite sets too—like all positive integers.'

slides.title: Counting Subsets
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'If a team has 11 players, how many different sub-teams can I form (including the full team and the empty team)?' Coach smiles: 'That's 2^11 = 2048 subsets. Every player is either in or out, so 2 choices per player × 11 players.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A team with n players has 2^n possible subsets (all combinations of including/excluding each player).

slides.title: Subsets and Equality
slides.storyContext: Arjun's team plays in three formats: Test cricket (5 players), ODI (8 players), T20 (11 players). Arjun notices: 'All Test players also play T20, but not all T20 players play Test.'

points.label: Subset
points.text: A ⊆ B means: every element of A is also in B.

points.label: Proper subset
points.text: A ⊂ B means A ⊆ B but A ≠ B (A is strictly smaller).

points.label: Equal sets
points.text: A = B if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A (they have the same elements).

example.solution: Yes, because every element of A (1 and 2) is in B. And A ⊂ B (proper subset) because A ≠ B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subset means all members of one group are also in a bigger group.

slides.title: Example: Cricket Format Subsets
slides.storyContext: Arjun records: T20 team = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram, Arjun, Rohan, Nikhil, Sameer, Ajay}. Test team = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak}.

example.problem: Is Test team ⊆ T20 team? Is it a proper subset?
example.solution: Yes, Test team ⊆ T20 team (every Test player is also in T20). And yes, it's a proper subset (⊂) because Test team ≠ T20 team (T20 has 11 players, Test has 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: The Test team is a proper subset of the T20 team because all Test players play T20, but T20 has more players.

slides.title: Union and Intersection
slides.storyContext: Two teams: Team A = {Raj, Karan, Priya} and Team B = {Karan, Deepak, Meera}. Priya asks: 'If both teams play together, who plays? Who is common to both?'

points.label: Union
points.text: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — all members of either or both.

points.label: Intersection
points.text: A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — members in both.

points.label: Disjoint sets
points.text: If A ∩ B = ∅, the sets share no elements.

example.solution: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4} (all elements from both). A ∩ B = {2, 3} (common elements).

slides.inSimpleWords: Union combines everything from both; intersection picks only what's in both.

slides.title: Team A and Team B Merge
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Team A has Raj, Karan, Priya. Team B has Karan, Deepak, Meera. If they play a mixed match together, it's the union—everyone plays. If they play 'only if in both teams', it's the intersection—only Karan plays.'

slides.title: Full Problem: Venn Diagram Application
slides.storyContext: In a school of 100 students, 60 play cricket, 40 play football, and 15 play both. How many play only cricket? How many play only football? How many play neither?

example.problem: Find the number in each region of a two-set Venn diagram.
example.solution: Let C = cricket players, F = football players. |C| = 60, |F| = 40, |C ∩ F| = 15. Only cricket: 60 − 15 = 45. Only football: 40 − 15 = 25. Both: 15. Neither: 100 − (45 + 25 + 15) = 15 students.

slides.inSimpleWords: Venn diagrams show overlaps clearly — count each region separately.

slides.title: Example: Cricket vs. Football at School
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to know: 'Of 100 students, 60 play cricket and 40 play football. How many play at least one?'

example.problem: Using union, find |C ∪ F| where |C| = 60, |F| = 40, |C ∩ F| = 15.
example.solution: |C ∪ F| = |C| + |F| − |C ∩ F| = 60 + 40 − 15 = 85. So 85 students play at least one sport.

slides.inSimpleWords: To count union, add both sets and subtract the overlap (to avoid double-counting).

slides.title: Venn Diagram in Action
slides.storyContext: Priya draws the Venn diagram on the board: two overlapping circles for C and F. 'See? The overlap region is C ∩ F. The left region (non-overlapping) is 'only cricket.' The right is 'only football.' And outside both is 'neither.' That's how we visualize set operations.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Venn diagrams make it visual: overlaps and regions show unions, intersections, and complements instantly.

slides.title: Complement and De Morgan's Laws
slides.storyContext: In Class 11A (total 50 students), the cricket team has 12 members. Coach asks: 'How many students are NOT on the cricket team?'

points.label: Complement
points.text: A' or A^c = {x | x ∉ A} — all elements NOT in A (within a universal set U).

example.solution: A' = {1, 3, 5} (all elements in U not in A).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complement is everything outside a set; De Morgan's laws flip unions and intersections when taking complements.

image.alt: Complement and De Morgan's Laws — Sets

slides.title: The Complement in Practice
slides.storyContext: Coach Ramesh tells the class: 'In Class 11A (50 students total), 12 are on the cricket team. So 50 − 12 = 38 are NOT on the team. That's the complement—everyone else.'

image.alt: The Complement in Practice — Sets

slides.title: De Morgan's Laws Explained
slides.storyContext: Priya works out a problem: 'If not (cricket or football), that means not cricket AND not football. That's De Morgan's law!' Coach nods. 'Exactly. (C ∪ F)' = C' ∩ F'. Taking a complement 'flips' unions to intersections.'
slides.inSimpleWords: De Morgan's laws: NOT(A or B) = NOT A and NOT B. NOT(A and B) = NOT A or NOT B. The 'not' flips the operation.

slides.title: Example: De Morgan's Laws in Sports
slides.storyContext: Let C = cricket players, F = football players, U = all students. If (C ∪ F)' is 'not playing any sport', then by De Morgan's, (C ∪ F)' = C' ∩ F' = 'not playing cricket AND not playing football'.

example.problem: If C = {Raj, Karan, Priya} (cricket) and F = {Karan, Deepak, Meera} (football), and U = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram}, find (C ∪ F)' and verify it equals C' ∩ F'.
example.solution: C ∪ F = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera}. (C ∪ F)' = {Vikram}. C' = {Deepak, Meera, Vikram}, F' = {Raj, Priya, Vikram}. C' ∩ F' = {Vikram}. Yes, they match!

slides.inSimpleWords: De Morgan's laws say: 'not playing cricket or football' = 'not playing cricket AND not playing football'.

image.alt: Example: De Morgan's Laws in Sports — Sets

slides.title: Challenge: Team Selection Logic
slides.storyContext: Arjun records: A = {players trained in batting}, B = {players trained in bowling}. Find the roster form if U = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram}, A = {Raj, Karan, Priya}, B = {Karan, Deepak, Meera}.

example.solution: (1) A ∪ B = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera}. (2) A ∩ B = {Karan}. (3) A' = {Deepak, Meera, Vikram}. (4) (A ∪ B)' = {Vikram}.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the operations step by step — first union, then intersection, then complement.

slides.title: Challenge: Three-Set Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun, Karan, and Priya each lead a team: A (batting), B (bowling), C (fielding). Priya asks: 'How many players are in none of these teams?'

example.problem: If A = {Raj, Karan, Priya}, B = {Karan, Deepak, Meera}, C = {Priya, Meera, Vikram}, and U = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram, Arjun}, find (A ∪ B ∪ C)'.
example.solution: A ∪ B ∪ C = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram}. (A ∪ B ∪ C)' = {Arjun}. Only Arjun is not in any team.

slides.inSimpleWords: For three sets, compute the union first, then take the complement of the entire union.

slides.title: Sets: Key Takeaways

points.text: A set is a well-defined, distinct collection of objects.
Represent sets in roster form {a, b, c} or set-builder form {x | condition}.
A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B (subset).
A ∪ B is union (all elements), A ∩ B is intersection (common elements).
A' is the complement (everything outside A in the universal set U).
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sets organize objects clearly; unions combine, intersections overlap, complements exclude.

slides.title: Why Sets Matter
slides.storyContext: Coach Ramesh wraps up: 'Sets are the foundation of all math. Without clear definitions and membership rules, we can't organize knowledge. Cricket, teams, groups, languages—everything relies on set thinking. You've just learned the building blocks of modern mathematics.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Sets teach you to organize, define boundaries, and think clearly—skills you'll use in every field.

subject: Mathematics
title: Pairing Students with Subjects: Relations and Functions
hook: When does a pairing rule become a true function? Arjun and Priya explore the rules.

slides.title: Subject Assignment at School
slides.storyContext: At Class 11A, Priya is assigned students to elective subjects. She tracks: 'Arjun takes Math, Karan takes Physics, Priya takes Math, Deepak takes Chemistry.' Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Is every student taking exactly one subject? Can one student take two subjects?' Priya realizes she needs to formalize this relationship.

image.alt: Subject Assignment at School — Relations and Functions

slides.title: The Pairing Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya writes on the board: 'Arjun → Math, Karan → Physics, Priya → Math.' Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Can Arjun take both Math and Physics?' Priya: 'No, each student takes one main elective.' Mrs. Sharma: 'Good. That's important. Let me show you how to formalize pairings.'

image.alt: The Pairing Problem — Relations and Functions

slides.title: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs
slides.storyContext: Priya writes all possible (student, subject) pairs on the board: (Arjun, Math), (Arjun, Physics), (Karan, Math), ...

points.label: Ordered pair
points.text: (a, b) is different from (b, a) — order matters.

points.label: Cartesian product
points.text: A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B} — all possible ordered pairs from A and B.

example.problem: If A = {Ram, Priya} and B = {Math, Physics}, list A × B.
example.solution: A × B = {(Ram, Math), (Ram, Physics), (Priya, Math), (Priya, Physics)}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Cartesian product pairs every element from the first set with every element from the second.

image.alt: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs — Relations and Functions

slides.title: Example: All Possible Subject Assignments
slides.storyContext: Priya lists all possible (student, subject) pairs: A = {Arjun, Karan}, B = {Math, Physics, Chemistry}.

example.problem: List A × B.
example.solution: A × B = {(Arjun, Math), (Arjun, Physics), (Arjun, Chemistry), (Karan, Math), (Karan, Physics), (Karan, Chemistry)}. Total: 2 × 3 = 6 pairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Cartesian product lists every possible combination, even ones that won't actually happen.

image.alt: Example: All Possible Subject Assignments — Relations and Functions

slides.title: What is a Relation?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma says: 'A relation is simply a subset of the Cartesian product — some (but not all) pairs from A × B satisfy a rule.'

points.label: Relation definition
points.text: R ⊆ A × B is a relation from A to B.

points.label: Domain
points.text: The set of all first elements in R — the 'input' set.

points.label: Codomain
points.text: The set B (the intended 'output' set).

points.label: Range
points.text: The set of all second elements actually appearing in R — subset of codomain.

example.problem: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and R = {(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8)} (the 'double' relation). Find domain, codomain, range.
example.solution: Domain = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Codomain = ℕ (all natural numbers, assumed). Range = {2, 4, 6, 8}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation picks some pairs from a Cartesian product according to a rule.

slides.title: Arjun's Subject Relation
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma says: 'Priya, you have a relation: {(Arjun, Math), (Karan, Physics), (Priya, Math), (Deepak, Chemistry)}. This is a subset of A × B. But notice: Arjun and Priya both map to Math. That's allowed in a relation.'

slides.title: What is a Function?
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Wait — can one student take two subjects at the same time?' Mrs. Sharma: 'If we're assigning ELECTIVES, each student takes exactly one. That's a function.'

points.label: Function definition
points.text: f: A → B is a relation where EVERY element of A maps to EXACTLY ONE element of B.

points.label: Notation
points.text: f(x) = y means the element x maps to y.

points.label: Test
points.text: A relation R is a function if no element of domain appears twice in the pairs.

example.solution: No — 1 maps to both 2 and 4. Each input must have exactly one output.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function gives each input exactly one output — no input can have two answers.

slides.title: Example: Valid Elective Assignment
slides.storyContext: Priya checks: 'Is 'each student assigned exactly one elective' a function?'

example.problem: f: {Arjun, Karan, Priya, Deepak} → {Math, Physics, Chemistry} with f(Arjun) = Math, f(Karan) = Physics, f(Priya) = Math, f(Deepak) = Chemistry. Is f a function?
example.solution: Yes. Every student (input) is assigned exactly one subject (output). Two students (Arjun, Priya) can have the same output (Math), and that's fine.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function ensures each input has one output, but multiple inputs can share the same output.

slides.title: Types of Functions: Injective, Surjective, Bijective
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Can two students take the same subject? Can a subject have no student?' Mrs. Sharma introduces three types.

points.label: Injective (one-to-one)
points.text: If f(a) = f(b), then a = b. Different inputs → different outputs.

points.label: Surjective (onto)
points.text: Every element of B is the image of some element in A (range = codomain).

points.label: Bijective
points.text: Both injective and surjective — a perfect one-to-one matching.

example.problem: f: {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c} with f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c. Is f bijective?
example.solution: Yes — f is injective (each input maps to a different output) and surjective (every element in codomain is hit). So f is bijective.

slides.inSimpleWords: Injective = no sharing outputs; surjective = all outputs are used; bijective = both.

slides.title: Three Types of Subject Assignments
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma explains: 'Suppose we have 3 students and 3 subjects. If each student gets a different subject AND each subject has exactly one student, that's a bijection. If two students can take Math, it's not injective. If Chemistry has no student, it's not surjective.'

slides.title: Composition of Functions
slides.storyContext: Arjun takes subject Math (function f), which has a difficulty level: Math → Level 3 (function g). Priya asks: 'What if I combine the two assignments?'

points.label: Composition
points.text: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) — apply f first, then g to the result.

points.label: Condition
points.text: f: A → B and g: B → C, then g ∘ f: A → C.

points.label: Order matters
points.text: f ∘ g is usually different from g ∘ f (not commutative).

example.problem: f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 3. Find (g ∘ f)(5) and (f ∘ g)(5).

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition chains functions — output of the first becomes input of the second.

slides.title: Example: Subject to Difficulty Composition
slides.storyContext: Let f: student → subject, and g: subject → difficulty. Then g ∘ f: student → difficulty.

example.problem: f(Arjun) = Math, g(Math) = 7. Find (g ∘ f)(Arjun).
example.solution: (g ∘ f)(Arjun) = g(f(Arjun)) = g(Math) = 7. So Arjun has difficulty level 7 (through Math).

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition lets you chain mappings: student → subject → difficulty in one step.

slides.title: Inverse Functions
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma: 'If Arjun's Math assignment is f, can we reverse it? If we know his subject is Math, can we get Arjun back?'

points.label: Inverse function
points.text: f⁻¹: B → A exists only if f is bijective.

points.label: Property
points.text: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(y)) = y.

points.label: Finding inverse
points.text: Set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, swap variables.

example.problem: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f⁻¹.
example.solution: Set y = 2x + 3. Solve: x = (y − 3)/2. Swap: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: An inverse function 'undoes' the original — if f sends x to y, f⁻¹ sends y back to x.

slides.title: Reversing the Assignment
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Can we reverse the subject assignment? If I know Arjun took Math, can I go backwards to find which student took it?' Mrs. Sharma: 'Only if each subject has exactly one student—a bijection. Then yes, we can invert.'

slides.title: Full Problem: Verifying Bijection and Finding Inverse
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma defines f: {1, 2, 3} → {5, 7, 9} by f(x) = 2x + 3. She asks: 'Is f bijective? Find f⁻¹.'

example.problem: Check if f is injective and surjective, then find f⁻¹.
example.solution: f(1) = 5, f(2) = 7, f(3) = 9. All different (injective). All elements {5, 7, 9} are hit (surjective). So f is bijective. f⁻¹(5) = 1, f⁻¹(7) = 2, f⁻¹(9) = 3, or f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify bijection, check that every input has one output and every output comes from one input.

slides.title: Challenge: Composition and Injectivity
slides.storyContext: Given f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, find (f ∘ g) and (g ∘ f). Verify that both are injective.

example.problem: Compute (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x). Are both injective?
example.solution: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(2x) = 2x + 1. (g ∘ f)(x) = g(x + 1) = 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2. Both are injective because if 2x₁ + 1 = 2x₂ + 1, then x₁ = x₂.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check injectivity by assuming f(a) = f(b) and proving a = b.

slides.title: Challenge: Three Functions Chain
slides.storyContext: Let f: students → subjects, g: subjects → difficulty, h: difficulty → time-needed. Find (h ∘ g ∘ f).

example.problem: If f(Arjun) = Math, g(Math) = 7, h(7) = 14 hours, find (h ∘ g ∘ f)(Arjun).
example.solution: (h ∘ g ∘ f)(Arjun) = h(g(f(Arjun))) = h(g(Math)) = h(7) = 14 hours. Arjun needs 14 hours to master Math.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chaining three functions: apply the innermost first, then work outward.

slides.title: Identity Function
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma introduces: 'There's a special function: the identity function, I(x) = x. It maps every element to itself. (I ∘ f)(x) = f(x) — composing with identity doesn't change anything.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The identity function maps x → x. Composing with it doesn't change the original function.

slides.title: Example: Verifying an Inverse
slides.storyContext: If f(x) = 3x − 2, verify that f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3 by showing f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

example.problem: Show that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for f(x) = 3x − 2.
example.solution: f(f⁻¹(x)) = f((x + 2)/3) = 3((x + 2)/3) − 2 = (x + 2) − 2 = x. Yes, the inverse works!

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify an inverse, compute f(f⁻¹(x)) and check that it equals x.

slides.title: Transformations via Functions
slides.storyContext: Functions can model transformations. If f: students → scores, then f is assigning scores. If g: scores → grades, then g assigns grades. Together, they 'transform' students into grades.

points.label: Transformation
points.text: A function transforms inputs into outputs via a rule.

points.label: Linear transformation
points.text: f(x) = mx + b transforms x by scaling and shifting.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: In coordinates, (x, y) → (x, mx + b) shifts and stretches the plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions transform inputs: scale them, shift them, reverse them—any rule that maps one set to another.

slides.title: Functions in the Real World
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes: 'Functions are everywhere. Temperature changes over time (time → temp). Marks map to grades (marks → grade). Prices depend on demand (demand → price). Every real-world relationship can be modeled as a function.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world relationships—temperature, grades, prices, distance—are all functions.

slides.title: Challenge: Modeling with Functions
slides.storyContext: A taxi charges: ₹50 base fare + ₹15 per km. Model this as a function and find the fare for 20 km.

example.problem: Let f(x) = 50 + 15x, where x = distance in km. Find f(20).

slides.inSimpleWords: Model real costs/prices as functions to predict outcomes instantly.

slides.title: Challenge: Composite Real Scenario
slides.storyContext: A laptop costs $100. Tax adds 10% (₹1 USD = ₹83). Find the final INR cost.

example.problem: f(x) = 1.1x (tax), g(x) = 83x (conversion). Cost = (g ∘ f)(100).

slides.inSimpleWords: Chaining real-world functions (tax, currency) compounds costs step by step.

slides.title: Functions: The Language of Relationships
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma concludes: 'Relations and functions are how we describe the world. Science, economics, engineering—all use functions to model how one thing depends on another. You've just learned the language of causality and dependence.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Functions describe all relationships: cause-and-effect, input-to-output, question-to-answer.

slides.title: Identity Function
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma introduces: 'There's a special function: the identity function, I(x) = x. It maps every element to itself. (I ∘ f)(x) = f(x) — composing with identity doesn't change anything.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The identity function maps x → x. Composing with it doesn't change the original function.

slides.title: Example: Verifying an Inverse
slides.storyContext: If f(x) = 3x − 2, verify that f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3 by showing f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

example.problem: Show that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for f(x) = 3x − 2.
example.solution: f(f⁻¹(x)) = f((x + 2)/3) = 3((x + 2)/3) − 2 = (x + 2) − 2 = x. Yes, the inverse works!

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify an inverse, compute f(f⁻¹(x)) and check that it equals x.

slides.title: Functions: The Language of Relationships
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma concludes: 'Relations and functions are how we describe the world. Science, economics, engineering—all use functions to model how one thing depends on another. You've just learned the language of causality and dependence.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Functions describe all relationships: cause-and-effect, input-to-output, question-to-answer.

slides.title: Relations and Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: A Cartesian product A × B is all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A, b ∈ B.
A relation is any subset of a Cartesian product.
A function f: A → B is a relation where every element of A maps to exactly one element of B.
Domain = inputs; codomain = intended outputs; range = actual outputs.
Injective = different inputs → different outputs. Surjective = all codomain elements are hit.
Bijective functions have inverses; composition chains functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions map each input to exactly one output; special types (injective, surjective, bijective) impose stronger conditions.
